title: 388. Geometry, Spatial Thinking & Measurement: Three-Dimensional Coordinate Distance
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.question: What is the distance between \((0,0,0)\) and \((1,2,2)\)?

questions.concept: Distance with an unchanged spatial coordinate
questions.learningObjective: Compute a spatial distance when one difference is zero.
questions.question: What is the distance between \((1,-2,3)\) and \((5,1,3)\)?
questions.explanation: The differences are \(4\), \(3\), and \(0\), so the distance is \(\sqrt{16+9}=5\).
questions.hint: A matching coordinate contributes zero to the squared distance.

questions.concept: Spatial distance with three nonzero differences
questions.question: What is the distance between \((-1,0,2)\) and \((2,4,14)\)?
questions.explanation: The differences are \(3\), \(4\), and \(12\). Thus the distance is \(\sqrt{9+16+144}=13\).
questions.hint: Square the coordinate differences before summing them.

questions.concept: Origin distance with a negative coordinate
questions.learningObjective: Compute a spatial norm with mixed signs.
questions.question: What is the distance from the origin to \((2,-3,6)\)?
questions.hint: Coordinate signs do not change their squared contributions.

questions.learningObjective: Keep an irrational three-dimensional distance exact.
questions.question: What is the distance between \((2,1,-3)\) and \((-1,3,1)\)?
questions.explanation: The differences are \(-3\), \(2\), and \(4\), so the squared distance is \(9+4+16=29\). Omitting the last coordinate gives \(13\).
questions.hint: Ensure that the third-coordinate difference is included.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a space diagonal from a face diagonal.
questions.question: A cube has edge length \(2\text{ cm}\). What is the distance between opposite vertices?
questions.explanation: Choose opposite vertices \((0,0,0)\) and \((2,2,2)\). Their distance is \(\sqrt{12}=2\sqrt{3}\text{ cm}\).
questions.hint: Opposite vertices differ along all three edge directions.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate a spatial diagonal from three side lengths.
questions.question: A rectangular box measures \(4\text{ cm}\) by \(4\text{ cm}\) by \(7\text{ cm}\). What is its body diagonal length?
questions.explanation: The body diagonal is \(\sqrt{4^2+4^2+7^2}=9\text{ cm}\). The value \(4\sqrt{2}\) is only the diagonal of the \(4\)-by-\(4\) face.
questions.hint: Include the height beyond the base-face diagonal.

questions.concept: Missing spatial coordinate with an inequality
questions.learningObjective: Select a spatial-distance solution using a directional constraint.
questions.question: The distance from \((1,2,3)\) to \((1,2,z)\) is \(6\), and \(z<3\). What is \(z\)?
questions.explanation: Only the third coordinate changes, so \(\lvert z-3\rvert=6\). The solutions are \(-3\) and \(9\); the inequality selects \(-3\).
questions.hint: Retain both possible directions until applying the inequality.

questions.learningObjective: Solve for a positive coordinate using a spatial norm.
questions.question: A point \((x,2,2)\), with \(x>0\), is at distance \(3\) from the origin. What is \(x\)?
questions.explanation: The equation is \(x^2+4+4=9\), giving \(x^2=1\). Positivity gives \(x=1\).

questions.learningObjective: Combine two distance conditions to recover a spatial coordinate.
questions.question: A point \(P=(x,t,4)\), with \(t>0\), is equally distant from \((0,0,0)\) and \((6,0,0)\). Its distance from the origin is \(13\). What is \(t\)?
questions.explanation: Equidistance gives \(x^2=(x-6)^2\), so \(x=3\). Then \(9+t^2+16=169\), giving \(t^2=144\) and \(t=12\).
questions.hint: Use equidistance to find the first coordinate before applying the full distance condition.
